name: Rocky Mountain National Park
blurb: Elk, willow and aspen, and a mountain food web in a warming climate.

tip.title: Shrink the snowpack
tip.text: Snowmelt waters meadows and streams. Cut Snowpack & snowmelt by 60% and watch willows and sedges, then the elk, moose and beaver that eat them.

sources.title: NPS: Mammals of Rocky Mountain National Park

notes: The story and why it matters come from the Wikipedia articles listed below (Rocky Mountain National Park, Elk, Moose). Individual species and links have not been checked one by one. Feeding links that match a GloBI (Global Biotic Interactions) record are marked in the node details, with a link to the records. A few links were added from GloBI records.

nodes.desc: Streamside shrubs of the montane valleys. The park page says elk overgrazing has damaged riparian areas, so some wetlands are fenced to let willows recover.

nodes.name: Quaking aspen
nodes.desc: A leafy tree of moister montane slopes. Elk like its spring sprouts, and groves have declined in places where elk are numerous.

nodes.name: Lodgepole pine
nodes.desc: A conifer that recolonizes old burn areas in the subalpine zone. It is a host of the mountain pine beetle.

nodes.name: Grasses & sedges
nodes.desc: Meadow and tundra grasses and sedges. Year-round food for elk, and pikas and marmots eat them too.
Reintroduced to the park in 1978 and now common, especially on the west side. Browses willow and birch shoots.

nodes.name: North American beaver
nodes.desc: A montane mammal that cuts woody stems for food and dams. Willow and aspen are typical foods.
Mostly a grazer that also browses. With wolves absent, the park culls some elk each winter and fences some wetlands from them.
A browsing deer and the main prey of the park's mountain lions, per the park page.
A small tundra and talus herbivore that stores dried plants as haypiles. It overheats in warm weather and relies on cool rock crevices.
A burrowing herbivore of meadows and rock slopes, listed among the park's mammals.
A very well-recorded park bird that eats carrion, seeds, berries and small animals.

nodes.name: American black bear
nodes.desc: An omnivore that is uncommon in the park (the park page gives only a few dozen). Eats plants, calves and carrion, and often visits cougar kills.
A widespread predator. Elk page notes coyotes mostly take calves, and pikas count coyotes among their predators.
A common soaring raptor of open country that hunts small mammals and birds.

nodes.name: Mountain lion
nodes.desc: The park's top predator, taking mostly mule deer, per the park page. Wikipedia lists elk and moose among cougar prey elsewhere.
Low-severity fire helps keep the forest in balance. The 2012 Fern Lake Fire burned nearly 3,500 acres after long fire-free years.
Thin mountain soils recycled from dead plants and animals feed forest, meadow and tundra plants.

nodes.name: Fungi & bacteria
nodes.desc: Break down dead wood, needles, plants and carcasses, returning nutrients to the soil.

story: Rocky Mountain National Park in Colorado sits on the Continental Divide, with 150 lakes and about 450 miles of rivers and streams. Its habitats run from wooded forest to mountain tundra. Elk, the second-largest deer species, live in its meadows and forests. The headwaters of the Colorado River are here.
matters: The Continental Divide gives the east and west sides of the park different climates. UNESCO made it one of the first World Biosphere Reserves in 1976.
